{{short description|American physicist (born 1946)}}
'''Robert Stetson Shaw''' (born 1946)<ref>[http://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n85093656.html LCCN]</ref> is an American [[physicist]] who was part of [[Eudaemons|Eudaemonic Enterprises]] in [[Santa Cruz, California|Santa Cruz]] in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 1988 he was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for his work in chaos theory.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.macfound.org/site/c.lkLXJ8MQKrH/b.1142699/k.7B86/Fellows_List__August_1988.htm |title=Fellows List - August 1988 |publisher=MacArthur Foundation |access-date=2010-02-06 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100212081433/http://www.macfound.org/site/c.lkLXJ8MQKrH/b.1142699/k.7B86/Fellows_List__August_1988.htm |archive-date=2010-02-12 }}</ref>

==Chaos theory==
Shaw was one of the pioneers of [[Chaos (physics)|chaos theory]] and his work at [[University of California, Santa Cruz]] on the subject was among the first research into the relationship between predictable motion and chaos in a landmark PhD thesis.<ref>Robert Shaw, ''The Dripping Faucet As a Model Chaotic System'', Science Frontier Express Series, Aerial Press, December 1984, December 1984 {{ISBN|0-942344-05-7}} [https://archive.org/details/ShawRobertDrippingFaucetAsAModelChaoticSystem1984_201811/mode/2up full text from archive]</ref>

He was part of the [[Dynamical Systems Collective]] with [[J. Doyne Farmer]], [[Norman Packard]], and [[James P. Crutchfield|James Crutchfield]]. The collective, also known as the Santa Cruz Chaos Cabal, was best known for its work in probing chaotic systems for signs of order.<ref>James Gleick, [[Chaos: Making a New Science]]</ref>

A documentary is being made about Shaw's life, his art, and his science, titled ''Strange Attractors: a movie for curious people''.<ref>''Strange Attractors: a movie for curious people'' (film)</ref>

==Roulette==
While at the University of California, Santa Cruz, Shaw also worked briefly with the [[Eudaemons]], a group of physicists attempting to create a [[computer]] capable of predicting the outcome of a game of [[roulette]].<ref>''The Eudaemonic Pie'' by Thomas A. Bass {{ISBN|0-595-14236-2}}</ref>

==Illustrations==
Shaw's younger brother, Chris, an artist and filmmaker, produced illustrations for Shaw's papers and thesis, and also for those of Shaw's PhD advisers [[Ralph Abraham (mathematician)|Ralph Abraham]] and [[William L. Burke|William Burke]]. One cosmological painting of consecutive universes exploding and imploding in alternating [[Big Bang]]s and [[Big Crunch]]es in Burke's cosmology textbook hangs on a wall at the [[American Center for Physics]].
